abstract: How the protein complexes and signal transduction pathways that regulate animal physiology and human disease emerged over evolutionary time remains poorly understood. The dystrophin-dystroglycan complex (DGC), whose disruption causes muscular dystrophy in humans, is best known for its role in maintaining muscle integrity and was previously thought to have originated in animals. Here we show that Capsaspora owczarzaki, a close unicellular relative of animals, encodes core DGC components- including a bona fide dystroglycan ortholog- as critical downstream targets of the Hippo pathway. Loss of Capsaspora dystrophin (coDystrophin) destabilizes the cortical actin cytoskeleton, causes excessive membrane blebbing, and produces flattened, irregularly shaped multicellular aggregates, all of which phenocopy loss of coYki. Conversely, coDystrophin overexpression rescues the cytoskeletal defects of coYki mutant cells, identifying coDystrophin as a key effector of Hippo signaling. Despite extensive rearrangement of dystrophin domain architecture during animal evolution, a human microdystrophin partially rescues coDystrophin mutant cells, revealing deep functional conservation. These findings show that core DGC components predate animals and indicate that the complex's ancestral role was not muscle-specific but lay in maintaining cortical cytoskeletal integrity under the control of an ancient Hippo-regulated genetic module.
